title: Constraints and NULL Values
description: Enforce data integrity with PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and CHECK constraints. Learn how NULL and three-valued logic work.

data.text: A database that accepts any garbage is a database that will give you garbage back. Constraints are rules you attach to tables and columns that tell SQL Server: 'reject any data that violates this rule.' They are your first line of defense for data quality.

NULL means 'unknown' or 'not applicable' — it is not zero, not an empty string, not a blank. It is the absence of a value. Because you don't know anything about an unknown value, SQL Server uses three-valued logic in comparisons: TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN.

data.title: NULL comparisons return UNKNOWN
data.content:
Assume column discount has the value NULL.

  price > 100    — evaluates to UNKNOWN (not TRUE or FALSE)
  price = NULL   — always UNKNOWN (use IS NULL instead)
  price <> 100   — also UNKNOWN

Because WHERE filters on TRUE only, rows with NULL in a compared column are excluded:

data.title: Testing for NULL correctly
data.code:
-- ✅ Correct way to find missing values
WHERE discount IS NULL

-- ❌ This finds nothing — NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, not TRUE
WHERE discount = NULL

data.title: NULL traps
data.text: You can never use = or <> to compare with NULL. Always use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. COUNT(*) counts rows including NULLs; COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values.

data.caption: Constraints protect data integrity at three levels — column, table, and cross-table
data.definition:
flowchart TD
  C[Constraints protect data] --> Col[Column-level]
  C --> Table[Table-level]
  C --> Cross[Cross-table]

  Col --> NN[NOT NULL]
  Col --> ID[IDENTITY]
  Col --> DFLT[DEFAULT]

  Table --> PK[PRIMARY KEY]
  Table --> UNIQ[UNIQUE]
  Table --> CK[CHECK]

  Cross --> FK[FOREIGN KEY]

data.text: SQL Server provides five main types of integrity constraints. Each one prevents a specific class of data problem.

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. By definition it cannot contain NULL, and only one primary key is allowed per table. When you define a primary key on a single column, SQL Server creates a clustered index on it by default.

data.title: Defining a primary key at table creation

data.text: A foreign key links a column (or columns) in one table to the primary key in another. It ensures that every 'child' value points to a valid 'parent' row — no orphaned references allowed.

data.title: Creating a foreign key relationship
data.code:
CREATE TABLE procurement.vendors (
    vendor_id   INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    vendor_name VARCHAR(100)    NOT NULL,
    group_id    INT             NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT fk_vendors_group
        FOREIGN KEY (group_id)
        REFERENCES procurement.vendor_groups(group_id)
);

data.title: Referential actions
data.text: When a parent row is deleted or updated, the foreign key can enforce different behaviors: ON DELETE CASCADE removes child rows automatically, ON DELETE NO ACTION raises an error, ON DELETE SET NULL clears the reference. Choose carefully based on your business rules.
By default, a column accepts NULL. Adding NOT NULL means every row must provide a value. This is how you ensure a 'last_name' field is never left blank.
UNIQUE ensures every value in a column (or combination of columns) is different. Unlike PRIMARY KEY, it allows one NULL. Behind the scenes, SQL Server creates a UNIQUE index to enforce it.

data.title: Adding a UNIQUE constraint

data.text: A CHECK constraint evaluates a boolean expression for every row. If the expression is false, the insert or update is rejected. This is where you encode business rules like 'discount must be between 0 and 1' or 'delivery date must be after the order date'.

data.title: Defining CHECK constraints
Key takeaways
points: NULL is 'unknown' — never compare with =; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL instead
PRIMARY KEY = unique + not null; one per table
FOREIGN KEY = referential integrity; use CASCADE or NO ACTION for deletes
NOT NULL = column must have a value
UNIQUE = no duplicates, allows one NULL; creates a UNIQUE index behind the scenes
CHECK = custom boolean rule, perfect for business logic like ranges
